structure.overview: The case concerns the Applicant from Bangladesh seeking judicial review of the Immigration Division's decision that found him inadmissible under IRPA sections 34(1)(f) and 34(1)(c) for membership in a terrorist organization. The Immigration Division concluded that the BNP and its affiliate JCD engaged in terrorism, but the Federal Court found the Division's reasoning on BNP's intent to cause serious harm insufficient and unreasonable. The Court granted the judicial review, set aside the inadmissibility finding, and remitted the matter to the Immigration Division for reconsideration by a new panel.

party_points.text: Admitted BNP membership but denied BNP is violent terrorist organization
JCD is BNP's creation and main actor in violence; BNP accountable for terrorism
Denied participation in violence or BNP's engagement in terrorism
Accepted violence during BNP hartals but denied BNP leadership intended injury or death
Certification question on whether repeated strikes causing harm can be terrorism under s.34(1)(c) IRPA

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant from Bangladesh seeks judicial review of the Immigration Division's decision finding him inadmissible under IRPA sections 34(1)(f) and 34(1)(c).

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c 27
citations.why: Defines grounds of inadmissibility cited in the decision

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant entered Canada on a student visa in April 2018 and applied for asylum in October 2018.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In November 2019, the Minister issued a report alleging reasonable grounds that the Applicant was a member of a terrorist organization, making him inadmissible under IRPA.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
citations.why: Legal basis for inadmissibility report

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Section 34 of the IRPA outlines security grounds for inadmissibility, including paragraphs 34(1)(c) and (f) concerning terrorism and membership in terrorist organizations.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c 27, s 34(1)(c), (f)
citations.why: Provides statutory text of security grounds for inadmissibility

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Minister's report states the BNP and JCD engaged in terrorist activities and implicitly organized violence to achieve political goals.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Minister referred the matter to the Immigration Division for an admissibility hearing held on April 13, 2021.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Minister's counsel presented documents to prove reasonable grounds that the Applicant was a JCD member and that BNP engaged in terrorism.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant admitted membership in BNP but denied that BNP is a violent terrorist organization.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Minister's counsel described Bangladesh's political history, noting BNP and Awami League as main parties with alternating election wins.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The AL government abolished caretaker government in 2011; BNP responded with strikes causing economic losses and street violence.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Documentary evidence shows BNP planned hartals causing violence including petrol bombings and railway damage.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: A 2009 article describes Bangladesh's political parties as having a culture of street violence.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Minister's counsel argued JCD is BNP's creation and main actor in violence, holding BNP accountable for resulting terrorism and requesting deportation.

citations.cite: Human Rights Watch report
citations.why: Supports claim of student wings' involvement in violence

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant admitted JCD membership for protection and resume benefit but denied attending meetings or rallies.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant denied voting for JCD candidates, participation in violence, or BNP's engagement in terrorism.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Immigration Division adopted the Supreme Court's Suresh definition of terrorism to conclude BNP and JCD engaged in terrorism.

citations.cite: Suresh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 SCC 1 at para 98
citations.why: Defines terrorism for the decision

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID noted BNP's absence from Canada's terrorist entity list is not determinative for terrorism under IRPA.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID used four factors from M.N. v Canada to assess BNP's engagement in terrorism: structure, leadership control, knowledge, and public stance.

citations.cite: M.N. v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2019 FC 796 at para 12
citations.why: Provides factors to assess terrorist organization status

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID agreed terrorism requires intent to cause serious harm and found the four M.N. factors met.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID concluded BNP had specific intent to cause death and serious harm, making Applicant inadmissible under IRPA 34(1)(f) and issued removal order.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The reasonableness standard applies to IRPA 34(1)(f) determinations of reasonable grounds for terrorist organization membership.

citations.cite: Intisar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 1128 at para 15
citations.why: States reasonableness standard for IRPA 34(1)(f) decisions

citations.cite: Miah v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2020 FC 38 at para 18
citations.why: Confirms reasonableness standard for such decisions

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Supreme Court in Vavilov defines a reasonable decision as rational, logical, and justified by law and facts, with traceable reasoning.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 102, 105
citations.why: Defines reasonableness standard for judicial review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The issue is whether the ID reasonably found reasonable grounds that BNP/JCD engages in terrorism under IRPA 34(1)(c).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Both parties agree that intent to cause death or serious harm is essential to define terrorism under IRPA 34(1)(c).

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant accepts violence occurred during BNP hartals but denies BNP leadership intended injury or death.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The question is whether the ID properly applied the Suresh terrorism definition and found BNP intended harm by calling hartals.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The reasonableness of intent findings in terrorism cases is debated, as noted by Justice Pentney in Babu v Canada.

citations.cite: Babu v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2022 FC 510 at para 26
citations.why: Notes judicial division on intent issue in terrorism cases

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Consensus is that proof of intent requires more than awareness or wilful blindness to likely violence from hartals.

citations.cite: Saleheen v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2019 FC 145 at para 41
citations.why: Clarifies intent proof requires more than awareness

citations.cite: Miah v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2020 FC 38 at para 34
citations.why: Supports higher standard for intent proof

citations.cite: Islam v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2021 FC 108 at para 20
citations.why: Confirms intent requires more than wilful blindness

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID found BNP planned violent hartals with leadership control, knowledge of violence risk, implicated leaders, and weak denunciation of violence.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The ID summarized findings at paragraphs 71-74 and reached a conclusion on BNP's terrorist activities.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the critical finding conclusory and lacking analysis on how it was reached.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The ID ignores BNP's legitimacy and the political context of hartals, which are common protest tools not inherently terrorist acts.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reports of violence during BNP hartals do not prove BNP engaged in terrorism or conclude so.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No evidence shows BNP leadership instructed violent acts; a link between violence and BNP intent is unproven.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The ID wrongly applied a lower standard of intent than required by law for calling hartals causing death or injury.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds Justice Norris's reasoning in Rana v Canada relevant to this case's circumstances.

citations.cite: Rana v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2018 FC 1080 at para 66
citations.why: Justice Norris's reasoning applies to this case

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applying Justice Norris's reasoning, the court concludes the BNP membership inadmissibility finding cannot be sustained.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The judicial review application is granted and the matter is remitted to the ID for reconsideration by a new panel.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Minister submits a certification question about whether repeated general strikes causing harm can be terrorism under s.34(1)(c) IRPA.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects the Minister's certification question as it concerns fact-based intent, not a general legal issue.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The member erred by equating hartals and blockades with terrorist activity without proving intent to cause serious harm as required.

citations.cite: Suresh
citations.why: Defines terrorism's essence as intent to cause serious harm

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The BNP is a legal political party whose leadership plans and coordinates hartals requiring mobilization and resources.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: BNP leadership controls members and called blockades causing deaths and injuries, targeting minorities to pressure the government.

citations.cite: Exhibit C-28, page 212
citations.why: Evidence of attacks during BNP blockades

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: BNP leadership knew of violent consequences from hartals and continued calls despite media coverage and accusations against leaders.

citations.cite: Exhibit C-28
citations.why: Media reports on political violence

citations.cite: 2012 onward
citations.why: Timeframe of events

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Human rights groups urged BNP to condemn violence, but BNP only vaguely denounced it and blamed others, condoning violence.

citations.cite: Exhibit C-36, pp. 357 – 360
citations.why: Human Rights Watch report

citations.cite: Exhibit C-34, p. 351
citations.why: Amnesty International report

citations.cite: Exhibit C-28, p. 271
citations.why: Evidence of BNP's vague denunciations

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The tribunal finds BNP had specific intent to cause death or serious harm, meeting the M.N. case factors for terrorism.

citations.cite: M.N.
citations.why: Factors for establishing specific intent in terrorism cases
